question_text:
An 82-year-old woman from a nursing home in Toowoomba, Qld, is brought in with three days of increasing drowsiness. She has type 2 diabetes treated with metformin. She is drowsy but rousable. Pulse 112/min, blood pressure 98/60 mmHg, dry mucous membranes.

Investigations:
- Blood glucose 46 mmol/L
- Sodium 149 mmol/L (135–145)
- Calculated serum osmolality 352 mOsm/kg (275–295)
- Capillary ketones 0.6 mmol/L (<0.6)
- Venous pH 7.34, bicarbonate 21 mmol/L

Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Fixed-rate insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/h started immediately alongside fluids
Intravenous 0.45% sodium chloride as the first fluid because sodium is raised
Intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride, starting a fixed-rate insulin infusion only once glucose stops falling with fluids
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Intravenous 0.9% sodium chloride, starting a fixed-rate insulin infusion only once glucose stops falling with fluids

---

This is hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS) without significant ketonaemia or acidosis. Fluid replacement with 0.9% sodium chloride comes first; fluids alone lower glucose. Starting insulin early can drive water into cells and cause circulatory collapse. The JBDS guideline advises giving fluids first and starting a fixed-rate infusion at 0.05 units/kg/h only once glucose has stopped falling, unless there is significant ketonaemia (mixed DKA/HHS).

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
In HHS, give 0.9% saline first and start low-dose insulin (0.05 units/kg/h) only once glucose stops falling, unless ketones are significant.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Joint British Diabetes Societies. Management of Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State (HHS) in Adults (updated guideline)", "url": "https://abcd.care/sites/default/files/site_uploads/JBDS_Guidelines_Current/JBDS_06_The_Management_of_Hyperosmolar_Hyperglycaemic_State_HHS_%20in_Adults_FINAL_0.pdf"}
subtopic: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state: fluids before insulin

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: This is DKA dosing. In HHS without ketosis, early or higher-dose insulin risks a fast osmolar shift and circulatory collapse.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Glucose-containing fluid is only added once glucose has fallen a long way. The first need is volume replacement with isotonic saline.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Hypotonic fluid is not the first-line choice. Isotonic saline restores volume, and osmolality should fall slowly (3–8 mOsm/kg/h).
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: She is not significantly acidotic. Bicarbonate has no role here.

key_takeaways: In HHS, give 0.9% saline first and start low-dose insulin (0.05 units/kg/h) only once glucose stops falling, unless ketones are significant.
guideline_reference: {"name": "Joint British Diabetes Societies. Management of Hyperosmolar Hyperglycaemic State (HHS) in Adults (updated guideline)", "url": "https://abcd.care/sites/default/files/site_uploads/JBDS_Guidelines_Current/JBDS_06_The_Management_of_Hyperosmolar_Hyperglycaemic_State_HHS_%20in_Adults_FINAL_0.pdf"}

question_text:
A 46-year-old woman presents to a Brisbane emergency department four hours after taking an unknown number of her mother's gliclazide modified-release tablets. On arrival her blood glucose was 2.1 mmol/L and she was given 50 mL of 50% glucose IV. A 10% glucose infusion was then started. Over the next two hours her glucose falls to 3.2 mmol/L twice despite the infusion. She is alert and her observations are otherwise normal.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next treatment?
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Octreotide

---

Sulfonylureas trigger ongoing insulin release, and repeated glucose boluses make it worse by stimulating more secretion. Octreotide suppresses insulin release. Queensland Poisons Information Centre antidote guidance recommends octreotide for sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia (BSL <4.0 mmol/L) after the first glucose correction.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Recurrent hypoglycaemia after a sulfonylurea overdose needs octreotide, which blocks insulin release, rather than more glucose boluses.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Queensland Poisons Information Centre. Antidote stocking recommendations: Octreotide", "url": "https://www.poisonsinfo.health.qld.gov.au/for-health-professionals/antidote-stocking-recommendations/octreotide"}
subtopic: Sulfonylurea overdose: octreotide for recurrent hypoglycaemia

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Repeated boluses stimulate further insulin release from the sulfonylurea-primed pancreas and cause rebound hypoglycaemia.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Glucagon has a brief effect, relies on liver glycogen and also stimulates insulin release. It is not the treatment for sulfonylurea toxicity.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Corticosteroids have no role in treating sulfonylurea-induced hyperinsulinaemia.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Charcoal may be considered early in a cooperative patient, but it does not treat the hypoglycaemia that is already happening.

key_takeaways: Recurrent hypoglycaemia after a sulfonylurea overdose needs octreotide, which blocks insulin release, rather than more glucose boluses.
guideline_reference: {"name": "Queensland Poisons Information Centre. Antidote stocking recommendations: Octreotide", "url": "https://www.poisonsinfo.health.qld.gov.au/for-health-professionals/antidote-stocking-recommendations/octreotide"}

question_text:
A 38-year-old man sees his GP in Geelong, Vic. He injected drugs 10 years ago. HCV antibody is positive and HCV RNA is detectable (genotype 3). He has never been treated. His APRI score is 0.3, liver function tests are mildly raised, and there is no clinical evidence of cirrhosis. He is not taking other medicines and is HIV and hepatitis B surface antigen negative.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Pegylated interferon with ribavirin for 24 weeks
Repeat HCV RNA in 6 months before deciding on treatment
Referral for liver biopsy before treatment
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Sofosbuvir/velpatasvir daily for 12 weeks

---

Australian hepatitis C guidelines recommend pan-genotypic direct-acting antivirals, either sofosbuvir/velpatasvir for 12 weeks or glecaprevir/pibrentasvir for 8 weeks. GPs can prescribe these. Genotyping is not required before treatment, and an APRI under 1 makes cirrhosis unlikely.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Treat chronic HCV in primary care with a pan-genotypic DAA: sofosbuvir/velpatasvir for 12 weeks or glecaprevir/pibrentasvir for 8 weeks.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Australian recommendations for the management of hepatitis C virus infection: recommended pan-genotypic treatment protocols", "url": "https://hepcguidelines.org.au/treatment-for-chronic-hepatitis-c/recommended-pan-genotypic-treatment-protocols/"}
subtopic: Chronic hepatitis C without cirrhosis: pan-genotypic DAA

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Interferon-based treatment is obsolete. It is less effective and more toxic than DAAs.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Glecaprevir/pibrentasvir is given for 8 weeks in treatment-naive patients. 24 weeks is not the recommended duration.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Chronic infection is already confirmed. Everyone with chronic HCV should be offered treatment now.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Biopsy is not needed. Non-invasive assessment such as APRI or elastography is used to stage fibrosis.

key_takeaways: Treat chronic HCV in primary care with a pan-genotypic DAA: sofosbuvir/velpatasvir for 12 weeks or glecaprevir/pibrentasvir for 8 weeks.
guideline_reference: {"name": "Australian recommendations for the management of hepatitis C virus infection: recommended pan-genotypic treatment protocols", "url": "https://hepcguidelines.org.au/treatment-for-chronic-hepatitis-c/recommended-pan-genotypic-treatment-protocols/"}

question_text:
A 34-year-old woman in Hobart, Tas, has had drooping of her left eyelid and double vision for six weeks. Both are worse in the evenings and after reading. On examination she has left ptosis that worsens with sustained upgaze for 60 seconds and variable diplopia. Pupils are equal and reactive. Limb power, reflexes and sensation are normal.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial investigation to confirm the likely diagnosis?
options: Lumbar puncture for CSF oligoclonal bands
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Serum acetylcholine receptor antibodies

---

Fatigable ptosis and diplopia with normal pupils suggest myasthenia gravis. Serum acetylcholine receptor antibodies are the first diagnostic test. They are found in most generalised cases and about half of purely ocular cases. Anti-MuSK antibodies, repetitive nerve stimulation or single-fibre EMG come next if AChR antibodies are negative. CT of the chest is then needed to look for a thymoma.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Fatigable ptosis or diplopia with spared pupils points to myasthenia gravis. Test serum AChR antibodies first.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Australian Prescriber. Myasthenia gravis (Therapeutic Guidance)", "url": "https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/"}
subtopic: Fatigable ptosis and diplopia: AChR antibody

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: MRI is used if there are signs of a brainstem lesion or if pupils are involved. It does not confirm myasthenia.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: CSF findings are normal in myasthenia. This test is for demyelination.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: CK is normal in myasthenia. It is raised in myopathies.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Standard NCS are normal in myasthenia. Repetitive stimulation, not F-waves, is the relevant neurophysiology test.

key_takeaways: Fatigable ptosis or diplopia with spared pupils points to myasthenia gravis. Test serum AChR antibodies first.
guideline_reference: {"name": "Australian Prescriber. Myasthenia gravis (Therapeutic Guidance)", "url": "https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/"}

question_text:
A 27-year-old woman in Adelaide, SA, has had pain on moving her right eye and blurred central vision for four days. Visual acuity is 6/36 right and 6/6 left. She has a right relative afferent pupillary defect and reduced red colour saturation, and the right optic disc looks normal. Two years ago she had three weeks of numbness from the waist down that resolved without treatment.

Which one of the following findings would most strongly support a diagnosis of multiple sclerosis?
options: A normal optic disc on fundoscopy
Periventricular and juxtacortical T2 lesions on MRI brain, with one lesion enhancing with gadolinium
A visual evoked potential with prolonged latency in the right eye
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Periventricular and juxtacortical T2 lesions on MRI brain, with one lesion enhancing with gadolinium

---

She has typical demyelinating optic neuritis after an earlier episode suggestive of a spinal cord lesion. MS is diagnosed by showing dissemination in space and time (McDonald criteria). Lesions in typical locations (periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial or spinal) show dissemination in space. Having enhancing and non-enhancing lesions at the same time shows dissemination in time.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
In optic neuritis, MRI brain lesions in typical MS locations, with both enhancing and non-enhancing lesions, satisfy dissemination in space and time.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Thompson AJ et al. Diagnosis of multiple sclerosis: 2017 revisions of the McDonald criteria. Lancet Neurol 2018;17:162-173", "url": "https://doi.org/10.1016/S1474-4422(17)30470-2"}
subtopic: Optic neuritis: MRI predicts MS risk

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Retrobulbar neuritis usually shows a normal disc. This fits optic neuritis but says nothing about MS.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: This confirms demyelination of the affected nerve that is already clinically apparent, but adds no evidence of spread elsewhere.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: AQP4 antibodies indicate neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder, which is a different condition from MS.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: ESR is non-specific. A raised value would make you think of giant cell arteritis or another inflammatory cause, not MS.

key_takeaways: In optic neuritis, MRI brain lesions in typical MS locations, with both enhancing and non-enhancing lesions, satisfy dissemination in space and time.
guideline_reference: {"name": "Thompson AJ et al. Diagnosis of multiple sclerosis: 2017 revisions of the McDonald criteria. Lancet Neurol 2018;17:162-173", "url": "https://doi.org/10.1016/S1474-4422(17)30470-2"}

question_text:
A 78-year-old woman in Bendigo, Vic, is seen by her GP because her daughter has noticed she is slower and shuffling. Over the past two months she has developed a symmetrical resting tremor, bradykinesia and rigidity in both arms. She has gastroparesis and started regular metoclopramide 10 mg three times daily three months ago. She has no other new medicines.

Which one of the following is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
options: Dopamine D2 receptor blockade by metoclopramide
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Dopamine D2 receptor blockade by metoclopramide

---

Symmetrical parkinsonism starting soon after a dopamine antagonist is typical of drug-induced parkinsonism. Metoclopramide is a common cause, especially in older women. The treatment is to stop the drug. Recovery may take weeks to months.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Symmetrical parkinsonism after starting metoclopramide is drug-induced (D2 blockade). Stop the drug.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Australian Prescriber. Drug-induced movement disorders", "url": "https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/"}
subtopic: Drug-induced parkinsonism from metoclopramide

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Idiopathic Parkinson disease is usually asymmetrical at onset. A symmetrical onset that follows a dopamine blocker points to the drug.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Essential tremor is a postural or action tremor without bradykinesia or rigidity.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: NPH causes gait apraxia with urinary incontinence and cognitive decline, not a resting tremor with arm rigidity.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: PSP causes early falls and a vertical gaze palsy, and it does not follow a new drug.

key_takeaways: Symmetrical parkinsonism after starting metoclopramide is drug-induced (D2 blockade). Stop the drug.
guideline_reference: {"name": "Australian Prescriber. Drug-induced movement disorders", "url": "https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/"}

question_text:
A 69-year-old man with severe COPD (FEV1 32% predicted) is brought by ambulance to a hospital in Launceston, Tas, with three days of increasing breathlessness and purulent sputum. Paramedics started oxygen at 15 L/min by non-rebreather mask. His SpO2 is now 99%, respiratory rate 24/min and he is drowsy.

Venous blood gas: pH 7.29, pCO2 68 mmHg.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate immediate change to his oxygen therapy?
options: Continue 15 L/min because he is hypoxic from the exacerbation
Change to nasal prongs at 6 L/min aiming for SpO2 above 94%
Give IV sodium bicarbonate to correct the acidosis
Titrate oxygen by Venturi mask to a target SpO2 of 88–92%
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Titrate oxygen by Venturi mask to a target SpO2 of 88–92%

---

High-flow oxygen in COPD can worsen hypercapnia (through V/Q mismatch and the Haldane effect). His drowsiness and acidosis point to this. COPD-X recommends controlled oxygen titrated to SpO2 88–92%, with blood gases repeated. He will also need non-invasive ventilation if the acidosis persists.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
In a COPD exacerbation, titrate oxygen to SpO2 88–92%. Over-oxygenation worsens hypercapnic acidosis.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Lung Foundation Australia. COPD-X Plan: X – Manage exacerbations", "url": "https://copdx.org.au/copd-x-plan/x-manage-exacerbations/"}
subtopic: COPD exacerbation: target SpO2 88–92%

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: An SpO2 of 99% is well above target, and the high-flow oxygen is contributing to his hypercapnic acidosis.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Stopping oxygen abruptly can cause dangerous rebound hypoxaemia. Titrate to target instead.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: This target is too high for a COPD patient with hypercapnia.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Respiratory acidosis is managed by controlling oxygen and supporting ventilation, not with bicarbonate.

key_takeaways: In a COPD exacerbation, titrate oxygen to SpO2 88–92%. Over-oxygenation worsens hypercapnic acidosis.
guideline_reference: {"name": "Lung Foundation Australia. COPD-X Plan: X – Manage exacerbations", "url": "https://copdx.org.au/copd-x-plan/x-manage-exacerbations/"}

question_text:
A 26-year-old man who has sex with men attends a sexual health clinic in Darlinghurst, NSW, for review of results from his routine screen. He has no symptoms. His pharyngeal swab NAAT is positive for Neisseria gonorrhoeae; urine and anorectal NAATs are negative. He has no drug allergies.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM plus azithromycin 1 g orally
Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 7 days
Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM plus azithromycin 2 g orally as a single dose
Ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally as a single dose
No treatment because he is asymptomatic
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM plus azithromycin 2 g orally as a single dose

---

The Australian STI Management Guidelines recommend ceftriaxone 500 mg IM with azithromycin for gonorrhoea. For pharyngeal infection the azithromycin dose is 2 g, rather than the 1 g used for uncomplicated genital or anorectal infection, because pharyngeal infection is harder to clear. A test of cure is recommended for pharyngeal infection.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
For pharyngeal gonorrhoea, give ceftriaxone 500 mg IM plus azithromycin 2 g, and arrange a test of cure.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Australian STI Management Guidelines. Gonorrhoea", "url": "https://sti.guidelines.org.au/sexually-transmissible-infections/gonorrhoea/"}
subtopic: Pharyngeal gonorrhoea: azithromycin 2 g with ceftriaxone

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: 1 g is the dose for genital or anorectal infection. Pharyngeal infection needs 2 g.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Doxycycline is a chlamydia treatment and is not adequate for gonorrhoea.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Resistance is common, so ciprofloxacin is not recommended empirically.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Asymptomatic pharyngeal gonorrhoea still transmits and should be treated, with contact tracing.

key_takeaways: For pharyngeal gonorrhoea, give ceftriaxone 500 mg IM plus azithromycin 2 g, and arrange a test of cure.
guideline_reference: {"name": "Australian STI Management Guidelines. Gonorrhoea", "url": "https://sti.guidelines.org.au/sexually-transmissible-infections/gonorrhoea/"}

question_text:
A 64-year-old woman on a medical ward in Darwin, NT, is being treated for community-acquired pneumonia with azithromycin. She also takes citalopram and has had diarrhoea for two days. Her monitor shows recurrent runs of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with a twisting QRS axis that end on their own. Between episodes she is alert, BP 122/74 mmHg, and her ECG shows sinus rhythm with a QTc of 590 ms.

Serum potassium is 3.1 mmol/L (3.5–5.2).

In addition to stopping QT-prolonging drugs and replacing potassium, which one of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment?
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Magnesium sulfate 2 g intravenously

---

This is torsades de pointes caused by an acquired long QT (macrolide, SSRI, hypokalaemia). IV magnesium sulfate (2 g, about 8 mmol, over 10–15 minutes) is first-line even when serum magnesium is normal. Also replace potassium to the high-normal range and stop the culprit drugs. If torsades continues, the next options are overdrive pacing or isoprenaline. Defibrillate if she becomes pulseless.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Treat torsades de pointes with IV magnesium, correct potassium and stop QT-prolonging drugs. Avoid amiodarone and sotalol.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Australian Resuscitation Council. Guideline 11.9: Managing acute dysrhythmias", "url": "https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-9-managing-acute-dysrhythmias"}
subtopic: Torsades de pointes: IV magnesium

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Amiodarone prolongs the QT interval further and can make torsades worse.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Sotalol is a class III drug that prolongs QT. It is contraindicated here.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: She is haemodynamically stable between self-limiting runs. Polymorphic VT cannot be synchronised. Defibrillate if she loses her pulse.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Beta-blockers are used for congenital long QT syndromes, not as acute treatment of acquired torsades.

key_takeaways: Treat torsades de pointes with IV magnesium, correct potassium and stop QT-prolonging drugs. Avoid amiodarone and sotalol.
guideline_reference: {"name": "Australian Resuscitation Council. Guideline 11.9: Managing acute dysrhythmias", "url": "https://www.anzcor.org/home/adult-advanced-life-support/guideline-11-9-managing-acute-dysrhythmias"}

question_text:
A 55-year-old man in Ballarat, Vic, has had swelling of his legs for two months. He has no diabetes and takes no regular medicines. BP 136/84 mmHg, pitting oedema to the knees.

Investigations:
- Urine albumin:creatinine ratio 620 mg/mmol
- Serum albumin 22 g/L (35–50)
- Creatinine 88 µmol/L (60–110)
- Total cholesterol 9.1 mmol/L
- Urine microscopy: no red cell casts
- Hepatitis B, hepatitis C and HIV serology negative; ANA negative; complement normal
- Serum anti-phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R) antibodies: strongly positive

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Primary membranous nephropathy

---

Anti-PLA2R antibodies are highly specific for primary membranous nephropathy. It is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in middle-aged and older white adults. With a typical picture and preserved kidney function, a strongly positive titre can support the diagnosis even without a biopsy. Age-appropriate cancer screening is still advised.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Strongly positive anti-PLA2R antibodies in adult nephrotic syndrome point to primary membranous nephropathy.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "KDIGO 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Glomerular Diseases", "url": "https://kdigo.org/guidelines/gd/"}
subtopic: Nephrotic syndrome in an adult: anti-PLA2R and membranous nephropathy

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Minimal change is the main cause in children and can occur in adults, but it is not associated with PLA2R antibodies.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: FSGS is a common cause in adults, but PLA2R antibodies are negative.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: IgA nephropathy usually causes haematuria, often after an upper respiratory infection, and rarely causes heavy nephrotic syndrome.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: ANA is negative and complement is normal, which argues against lupus.

key_takeaways: Strongly positive anti-PLA2R antibodies in adult nephrotic syndrome point to primary membranous nephropathy.
guideline_reference: {"name": "KDIGO 2021 Clinical Practice Guideline for the Management of Glomerular Diseases", "url": "https://kdigo.org/guidelines/gd/"}

question_text:
A 31-year-old woman in Cairns, Qld, has had no periods for eight months and has noticed milky nipple discharge. A pregnancy test is negative. She is not taking any medicines. Visual field testing is normal.

Investigations:
- Serum prolactin 4,800 mIU/L (<500)
- TSH normal
- MRI pituitary: 14 mm sellar mass without chiasmal compression

Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Combined oral contraceptive pill to restore periods
Repeat MRI in 12 months with no treatment
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Cabergoline

---

A macroadenoma with prolactin this high is a prolactinoma. First-line treatment is a dopamine agonist, preferably cabergoline, even for macroadenomas and even when there are visual field defects. It normalises prolactin and shrinks the tumour in most patients. Surgery is kept for patients who don't respond or can't tolerate it.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Prolactinomas, including macroadenomas, are treated first with a dopamine agonist (cabergoline). Surgery is second-line.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Melmed S et al. Diagnosis and treatment of hyperprolactinemia: an Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline. J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2011", "url": "https://doi.org/10.1210/jc.2010-1692"}
subtopic: Macroprolactinoma: dopamine agonist first-line

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Surgery is second-line, for patients who are resistant to or intolerant of dopamine agonists.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Radiotherapy is reserved for aggressive tumours that have failed medical and surgical treatment.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: This treats the amenorrhoea but not the tumour.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: She has a symptomatic macroadenoma, which needs treatment.

key_takeaways: Prolactinomas, including macroadenomas, are treated first with a dopamine agonist (cabergoline). Surgery is second-line.
guideline_reference: {"name": "Melmed S et al. Diagnosis and treatment of hyperprolactinemia: an Endocrine Society clinical practice guideline. J Clin Endocrinol Metab 2011", "url": "https://doi.org/10.1210/jc.2010-1692"}

question_text:
A 72-year-old man in Orange, NSW, has had tingling in both feet for four months and feels more tired. He has had type 2 diabetes for 12 years treated with metformin 1 g twice daily. His HbA1c is 6.9%. He eats a mixed diet. There is reduced vibration sense at the toes.

Investigations:
- Haemoglobin 118 g/L (130–180)
- MCV 104 fL (80–100)
- Serum B12 105 pmol/L (>150)
- Folate normal
- TSH normal

Which one of the following is the most likely cause of his macrocytosis?
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Metformin-associated vitamin B12 malabsorption

---

Long-term metformin reduces B12 absorption in the ileum. B12 deficiency can cause macrocytic anaemia and a neuropathy that can be mistaken for diabetic neuropathy. B12 should be checked periodically in long-term metformin users, especially those with anaemia or neuropathy. He needs B12 replacement, and metformin can usually continue.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Long-term metformin can cause B12 deficiency, with macrocytosis and neuropathy. Check B12 in these patients.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "Australian Prescriber. Metformin and vitamin B12 deficiency (drug information)", "url": "https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/"}
subtopic: Long-term metformin: vitamin B12 deficiency

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: This is possible, and intrinsic factor antibodies could be checked, but long-term high-dose metformin is the most likely cause here.
incorrect_answer_explanations.B: He eats a mixed diet, so dietary deficiency is unlikely.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: TSH is normal.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Neuropathy alone does not explain macrocytic anaemia with a low B12.

key_takeaways: Long-term metformin can cause B12 deficiency, with macrocytosis and neuropathy. Check B12 in these patients.
guideline_reference: {"name": "Australian Prescriber. Metformin and vitamin B12 deficiency (drug information)", "url": "https://australianprescriber.tg.org.au/"}

question_text:
A 70-year-old woman presents to her GP in Mackay, Qld, with two days of burning pain over her right forehead followed by a vesicular rash in the distribution of the right ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve. Valaciclovir is started.

Which one of the following examination findings most strongly predicts eye involvement and the need for urgent ophthalmology review?
options: Vesicles on the tip of the nose
Rash extending to the scalp vertex
Pain over the forehead before the rash
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Vesicles on the tip of the nose

---

Hutchinson sign is vesicles on the tip, side or root of the nose. It means the nasociliary branch of V1 is involved, and that branch also supplies the cornea. It strongly predicts ocular herpes zoster (keratitis or uveitis). Any patient with HZO, and especially Hutchinson sign, red eye or reduced vision, needs prompt ophthalmology assessment with a slit lamp.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Hutchinson sign (vesicles on the nasal tip) means nasociliary involvement. Expect ocular zoster and refer urgently.

---

REFERENCES
• {"name": "RANZCO / Eye health resources", "url": "https://ranzco.edu/"}
subtopic: Herpes zoster ophthalmicus: Hutchinson sign

incorrect_answer_explanations.A: Eyelid involvement is common in HZO but predicts eye involvement less strongly than nasal tip lesions.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: Lymphadenopathy is non-specific.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: The vertex lies in the V1 dermatome via the supraorbital and supratrochlear branches, which do not supply the globe.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Prodromal pain is typical of shingles and does not predict eye involvement.

question_text:
A 58-year-old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis presents to an emergency department in Mildura, Vic, after vomiting about 500 mL of fresh blood. Pulse 118/min, BP 92/58 mmHg. Two large-bore cannulas are in place and crystalloid is running. Haemoglobin is 82 g/L. Endoscopy can be done in four hours.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate management before endoscopy?
options: Transfuse to a haemoglobin of 120 g/L before endoscopy
Intravenous terlipressin and intravenous ceftriaxone, with restrictive red cell transfusion to a haemoglobin of about 70–80 g/L
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Intravenous terlipressin and intravenous ceftriaxone, with restrictive red cell transfusion to a haemoglobin of about 70–80 g/L

---

Suspected variceal haemorrhage should be treated before endoscopy with a vasoactive drug (terlipressin or octreotide) and prophylactic antibiotics (such as ceftriaxone). The antibiotics reduce infection, rebleeding and death. A restrictive transfusion target of about 70–80 g/L is used because over-transfusion raises portal pressure. Endoscopic band ligation should follow within 12 hours.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
For a suspected variceal bleed, give terlipressin and IV antibiotics, transfuse restrictively, and arrange early band ligation.

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Balloon tamponade is a temporary rescue measure for uncontrolled bleeding, not first-line treatment.

question_text:
A 76-year-old man in Wagga Wagga, NSW, collapsed while walking up a hill and recovered within a minute. He has had increasing breathlessness on exertion for three months. He has an ejection systolic murmur at the right upper sternal edge radiating to the carotids, with a soft second heart sound. ECG shows sinus rhythm with left ventricular hypertrophy.

Which one of the following echocardiographic findings best indicates that he needs aortic valve intervention?
options: Peak velocity 2.8 m/s with a mean gradient of 18 mmHg
Aortic valve sclerosis without restricted leaflet opening
Peak aortic jet velocity 4.4 m/s with a mean gradient of 46 mmHg
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Peak aortic jet velocity 4.4 m/s with a mean gradient of 46 mmHg

---

Severe aortic stenosis is defined by a peak velocity of at least 4 m/s, a mean gradient of at least 40 mmHg or a valve area under 1.0 cm². When a patient with severe AS has symptoms (exertional syncope, angina or breathlessness), surgical or transcatheter valve replacement is indicated, because prognosis is poor without it.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Severe AS (≥4 m/s, mean gradient ≥40 mmHg, AVA <1.0 cm²) with symptoms is an indication for valve replacement.

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Sclerosis is not stenosis and does not need intervention.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: This does not explain his symptoms or carry the same indication.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: A preserved ejection fraction does not by itself indicate the need for intervention.

key_takeaways: Severe AS (≥4 m/s, mean gradient ≥40 mmHg, AVA <1.0 cm²) with symptoms is an indication for valve replacement.

question_text:
A 67-year-old man presents to an emergency department in Bunbury, WA, with eight hours of a painful lump in his right groin that will no longer go back in. He has had a reducible right inguinal hernia for two years. He has vomited twice. Temperature 37.9°C, pulse 104/min. The lump is tense, red and very tender, and no cough impulse can be felt. Lactate is 3.1 mmol/L.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Urgent surgical exploration and hernia repair
Manual reduction under opioid analgesia, then elective repair
Elective repair on the next available list
Ultrasound of the groin before deciding on management
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Urgent surgical exploration and hernia repair

---

A tender, irreducible, red hernia with fever, vomiting, tachycardia and a raised lactate suggests strangulation. Bowel viability is at risk, so he needs resuscitation and emergency surgery. Manual reduction should not be attempted when strangulation is suspected, because dead bowel could be pushed back into the abdomen.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
A tender, irreducible hernia with systemic signs is strangulated until proven otherwise. Do not reduce it; operate urgently.

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.C: This is an emergency.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: A truss has no role for an irreducible hernia.
incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Imaging should not delay surgery when the clinical diagnosis is clear.

key_takeaways: A tender, irreducible hernia with systemic signs is strangulated until proven otherwise. Do not reduce it; operate urgently.

question_text:
A 61-year-old man in Toowong, Qld, has a PSA of 6.8 µg/L on testing he chose after discussion with his GP. A repeat PSA six weeks later is 7.1 µg/L. Digital rectal examination finds a smooth, mildly enlarged prostate. He has no urinary symptoms and a urine dipstick is normal. He is referred to a urologist.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next investigation?
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Multiparametric MRI of the prostate

---

The 2026 Australian guidelines for early detection of prostate cancer recommend multiparametric MRI as the next test after a confirmed raised PSA, before any biopsy. Biopsy is recommended for PI-RADS 4–5, or for PI-RADS 3 with a PSA density of 0.15 or more. This approach avoids unnecessary biopsies and finds fewer insignificant cancers.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
After a confirmed raised PSA, the next test is mpMRI. Biopsy depends on the PI-RADS score and PSA density.

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.E: The PSA is confirmed raised and he needs further assessment now.

question_text:
A 24-year-old man was tackled during a rugby league match in Penrith, NSW, and now has left upper quadrant pain. At a major trauma centre, after 1 L of crystalloid, his pulse is 88/min and BP 128/76 mmHg and both are stable over two hours. CT with IV contrast shows a grade III splenic laceration with no contrast blush and a small amount of free fluid. He has no other injuries.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Admission for non-operative management with serial examination and haemoglobin monitoring
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Admission for non-operative management with serial examination and haemoglobin monitoring

---

In a haemodynamically stable patient without peritonitis, a grade I–III splenic injury without active extravasation is managed non-operatively at a centre that can operate or perform angioembolisation at short notice. Splenectomy is kept for haemodynamic instability. Angioembolisation is used for a contrast blush or a higher-grade injury.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Stable blunt splenic injury without a contrast blush: manage non-operatively with close monitoring.

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.E: There is no contrast blush, so embolisation is not needed at this point.

question_text:
A 35-year-old motorcyclist arrives at an emergency department in Albury, NSW, after a high-speed crash. He is agitated and in severe respiratory distress. Pulse 138/min, BP 78/40 mmHg, SpO2 82% on high-flow oxygen. The trachea is deviated to the left, his neck veins are distended, and the right chest is hyper-resonant with absent breath sounds.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate immediate action?
options: Urgent chest X-ray to confirm the diagnosis
Immediate decompression of the right chest without waiting for imaging
Rapid sequence intubation before any chest procedure
Bedside echocardiography to look for tamponade
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Immediate decompression of the right chest without waiting for imaging

---

This is a clinical diagnosis of tension pneumothorax, and it needs immediate decompression (needle or finger thoracostomy) followed by an intercostal catheter. In adults, the site taught in ATLS 10th edition is the 4th or 5th intercostal space just anterior to the mid-axillary line. Imaging must not delay treatment.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis. Decompress immediately; do not wait for imaging.

---

question_text:
A 22-year-old man fell onto his outstretched arm while skateboarding in Fremantle, WA. His right shoulder is squared off, he holds the arm slightly abducted and externally rotated, and there is a palpable fullness in front of the shoulder. Radial pulse is present.

Before reduction, which one of the following is the most important neurological assessment to document?
options: Sensation over the first dorsal web space
Sensation over the lateral aspect of the upper arm (regimental badge area)
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Sensation over the lateral aspect of the upper arm (regimental badge area)

---

Anterior dislocation can stretch the axillary nerve as it passes around the surgical neck of the humerus. Check its sensory supply over the lateral deltoid (the regimental badge area) and document it before and after reduction. Deltoid power cannot be tested reliably while the shoulder is dislocated.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
In anterior shoulder dislocation, document regimental badge sensation (axillary nerve) before and after reduction.

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.E: This tests the median nerve.

question_text:
A 74-year-old man who smokes presents to a regional emergency department in Dubbo, NSW, with sudden severe back and left flank pain and a brief collapse. Pulse 112/min, BP 86/54 mmHg. He is alert and talking. There is a tender pulsatile mass in the epigastrium. Bedside ultrasound shows an infrarenal aorta of 7.2 cm.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Give fluids to keep systolic BP above 120 mmHg before transfer
Permissive hypotension while he is alert, with immediate referral to vascular surgery for repair
CT angiogram first, with surgical referral only if rupture is confirmed
IV labetalol to lower blood pressure
Admit under general medicine for analgesia and serial ultrasound
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Permissive hypotension while he is alert, with immediate referral to vascular surgery for repair

---

Suspected ruptured AAA in a patient whose cerebration is preserved should be managed with permissive (controlled) hypotension. Avoid aggressive fluids, which dilute clotting factors and can dislodge the clot. Then arrange immediate transfer for endovascular or open repair. The ESVS 2024 guideline recommends permissive hypotension. A CT angiogram is only done if he is stable enough and it will not delay repair.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
For a ruptured AAA: permissive hypotension while he remains alert, and immediate vascular repair.

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.E: This is a surgical emergency.

question_text:
A 23-year-old man presents to a GP in Newcastle, NSW, with three days of right scrotal pain and swelling. Pain began gradually. He has a new female partner and does not use condoms. Temperature 37.8°C. The right epididymis is swollen and tender, the testis lies normally, and the cremasteric reflex is present. A urine NAAT for chlamydia and gonorrhoea has been sent. Ultrasound shows increased blood flow to the epididymis.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
options: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM single dose plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days
Ciprofloxacin 500 mg twice daily for 10 days
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM single dose plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days

---

In men under 35, epididymo-orchitis is most often caused by chlamydia or gonorrhoea. The Australian STI Management Guidelines recommend ceftriaxone 500 mg IM plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 14 days. Azithromycin 1 g repeated after one week is an alternative to doxycycline. Partners need to be notified and treated.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Epididymo-orchitis in a man under 35: ceftriaxone 500 mg IM plus doxycycline 100 mg BD for 14 days.

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.E: This does not cover gonorrhoea and is too short for epididymo-orchitis.

question_text:
A 56-year-old man in Rockhampton, Qld, has had severe epigastric pain for three hours that came on suddenly and is now generalised. He takes ibuprofen regularly for knee osteoarthritis. He is lying very still. Pulse 110/min, BP 108/70 mmHg, temperature 37.6°C. His abdomen is rigid with generalised guarding and absent bowel sounds. Lipase is 90 U/L (<60).

Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Perforated peptic ulcer

---

Sudden severe epigastric pain that becomes generalised peritonitis (a board-like abdomen in a patient lying still) in a regular NSAID user strongly suggests a perforated peptic ulcer. An erect chest X-ray may show gas under the diaphragm, and CT is more sensitive. Lipase can rise slightly with perforation. Pancreatitis usually gives a lipase more than three times normal.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Sudden epigastric pain with peritonitis in an NSAID user suggests a perforated peptic ulcer. Mild lipase rises can occur.

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: Biliary colic does not cause generalised peritonitis.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: An MI can cause epigastric pain but not a rigid abdomen.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: Mesenteric ischaemia causes pain out of proportion to examination findings early on. A rigid abdomen from the start fits perforation better.

question_text:
A 28-year-old woman presents to an emergency department in Bundaberg, Qld, with five days of worsening sore throat, now worse on the left. She can barely open her mouth, has a muffled 'hot potato' voice and is drooling. Temperature 38.6°C. Her airway is patent and SpO2 is 98% on room air. The left soft palate is swollen and the uvula is pushed to the right.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: Needle aspiration or incision and drainage, with IV benzylpenicillin
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Needle aspiration or incision and drainage, with IV benzylpenicillin

---

Trismus, a hot potato voice and a displaced uvula indicate a peritonsillar abscess (quinsy). It is treated by drainage (needle aspiration or incision), antibiotics (IV benzylpenicillin, plus metronidazole in some protocols), analgesia and fluids. Most patients do not need an immediate tonsillectomy.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Quinsy: drain (aspirate or incise) and give IV penicillin-based antibiotics.

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.E: Steroids may be used alongside other treatment, but they do not replace drainage.

question_text:
A 69-year-old woman is on the surgical ward in Townsville, Qld, on day 1 after an open right hemicolectomy. Her urine output has been 15 mL/h for four hours (weight 70 kg). Her IV fluids were reduced overnight. Pulse 106/min, BP 104/62 mmHg, capillary refill 4 seconds. Her catheter flushes freely.

Investigations:
- Creatinine 128 µmol/L (pre-op 72)
- Urea 14.2 mmol/L
- Urine sodium 9 mmol/L
- Fractional excretion of sodium 0.5%

Which one of the following is the most likely cause of her oliguria?
options: Prerenal acute kidney injury due to hypovolaemia
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Prerenal acute kidney injury due to hypovolaemia

---

She is tachycardic with slow capillary refill, her fluids were reduced, the catheter is patent, and her urine sodium (<20 mmol/L) and FENa (<1%) are low. This fits prerenal AKI: the tubules are working and avidly holding on to sodium. Give a fluid bolus and reassess. Urea is often disproportionately high in prerenal states.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Post-operative oliguria with low urine sodium and FENa below 1% is prerenal. Give fluid and reassess.

---

incorrect_answer_explanations.B: The catheter flushes freely.
incorrect_answer_explanations.C: A ureteric injury would not fit these urine indices or the fluid history.
incorrect_answer_explanations.D: She has a working catheter.

key_takeaways: Post-operative oliguria with low urine sodium and FENa below 1% is prerenal. Give fluid and reassess.

question_text:
A 24-year-old woman at 11 weeks' gestation is admitted to a hospital in Shepparton, Vic, after two weeks of persistent vomiting. She has kept almost nothing down for five days and has lost 6% of her body weight. Pulse 108/min. Urine ketones 3+.

Investigations:
- Sodium 136 mmol/L, potassium 3.2 mmol/L
- Glucose 3.9 mmol/L

IV fluids, potassium replacement and antiemetics are planned.

Which one of the following should be given before any glucose-containing IV fluid?
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Intravenous thiamine

---

After prolonged vomiting and poor intake, thiamine stores are depleted. Glucose can then precipitate Wernicke encephalopathy. The NSW Health 2022 guideline recommends IV thiamine 100 mg daily when oral intake is poor or IV glucose is needed. Glucose-containing fluids should only be used after thiamine has been given and hyponatraemia excluded. Rehydration uses 0.9% sodium chloride with potassium as needed.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
In hyperemesis with poor intake, give IV thiamine before glucose to prevent Wernicke encephalopathy.

---

question_text:
A 27-year-old woman presents to an emergency department in Mount Gambier, SA, with sudden severe right iliac fossa pain that began four hours ago while she was exercising, with vomiting. A beta-hCG is negative. She is very tender in the right adnexa. Pelvic ultrasound shows a 7 cm right ovarian cyst with an enlarged ovary, and Doppler shows arterial flow is present.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Urgent gynaecology review for diagnostic laparoscopy
Discharge because arterial flow is present
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Urgent gynaecology review for diagnostic laparoscopy

---

Sudden pain with vomiting and an enlarged ovary containing a cyst over 5 cm strongly suggests ovarian torsion. Doppler flow does not exclude torsion, because venous congestion comes before arterial loss. Torsion is a clinical diagnosis, and laparoscopy with detorsion is urgent to save the ovary.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Suspected ovarian torsion needs urgent laparoscopy. Normal Doppler flow does not exclude it.

---

question_text:
A 22-year-old woman sees her GP in Ipswich, Qld, with severe period pain for four years that is not controlled by regular NSAIDs. She also has pain with deep penetration. She does not want to become pregnant in the next few years. Pelvic examination is normal apart from mild posterior fornix tenderness, and a pelvic ultrasound is normal.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Reassure her because the ultrasound is normal
Start continuous combined oral contraceptive pill or a progestogen and review in three months
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Start continuous combined oral contraceptive pill or a progestogen and review in three months

---

The 2021 Australian endometriosis guideline (RANZCOG) supports empirical hormonal treatment for suspected endometriosis without requiring laparoscopy first. Options are combined oral contraception or progestogens (oral, implant or levonorgestrel IUD). Review after about three months and refer if symptoms persist. A normal ultrasound does not exclude endometriosis.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Suspected endometriosis can be treated empirically with COCP or progestogens. A normal ultrasound does not exclude it.

---

question_text:
A 19-year-old woman phones a clinic in Wollongong, NSW. She takes a combined oral contraceptive pill. She started her new pack three days ago, two days late after the hormone-free week, and has since missed the pills for day 2 and day 3. She had unprotected sex two nights ago. She feels well.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate advice?
options: Take a pill now; no other precautions needed
Stop the pack and start a new one next week
Take a pill now, use condoms for 7 days, and take emergency contraception
Take two pills now and use condoms for 2 days
Do a pregnancy test now and decide afterwards
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Take a pill now, use condoms for 7 days, and take emergency contraception

---

Family Planning NSW advice: a pill more than 24 hours late means taking the most recent missed pill, continuing the pack, and using condoms for 7 days. When more than one pill is missed in the first week of a pack (after the hormone-free interval) and there has been unprotected sex in the previous 5 days, emergency contraception is recommended.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
More than one pill missed in week 1 with unprotected sex in the past 5 days: take a pill, use condoms for 7 days, and take EC.

---

question_text:
A 29-year-old woman at 27+3 weeks' gestation presents to a tertiary hospital in Randwick, NSW, with regular painful contractions. Her cervix is 6 cm dilated, membranes are intact and fetal monitoring is normal. Birth is expected within hours. Betamethasone has been given.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate additional treatment?
options: Intravenous magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Intravenous magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection

---

When birth is planned or expected within 24 hours at 24 to under 30 weeks, magnesium sulfate is given for fetal neuroprotection. It reduces the risk of cerebral palsy. This is the indication in the SESLHD/RHW local guideline, which follows the Australian national guideline.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Give MgSO4 for fetal neuroprotection when birth is expected within 24 hours at 24 to under 30 weeks.

---

question_text:
A 44-year-old woman with three children sees her GP in Albany, WA, with urine leakage when she coughs, laughs or runs. It began after her last birth. She has no urgency or nocturia. Urinalysis is normal and her BMI is 31 kg/m². Pelvic examination shows no significant prolapse.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate first-line management?
options: Supervised pelvic floor muscle training for at least three months
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Supervised pelvic floor muscle training for at least three months

---

Supervised pelvic floor muscle training, for example with a women's health physiotherapist, for at least three months is first-line for stress urinary incontinence. Weight loss and managing cough or constipation help too. Surgery (such as colposuspension or autologous sling) is considered only after conservative treatment fails.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
First-line treatment for stress incontinence is supervised pelvic floor training for at least three months.

---

question_text:
A 33-year-old woman sees a GP in Canberra, ACT, after her third consecutive first-trimester miscarriage. Each was at 7–9 weeks. She has no other medical history. Her partner is well. Pelvic ultrasound is normal.

Which one of the following investigations is most likely to identify a treatable cause?
options: Inherited thrombophilia screen (factor V Leiden, protein C and S)
Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-β2-glycoprotein I antibodies, repeated after 12 weeks if positive
Serum progesterone in a non-pregnant cycle
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-β2-glycoprotein I antibodies, repeated after 12 weeks if positive

---

Antiphospholipid syndrome is the most important treatable cause of recurrent miscarriage. Testing includes lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin and anti-β2-glycoprotein I antibodies. Persistent positivity has to be confirmed 12 weeks apart. Treatment in a future pregnancy is low-dose aspirin with prophylactic heparin.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Recurrent miscarriage: test for antiphospholipid syndrome, confirm at 12 weeks, and treat with aspirin plus heparin in the next pregnancy.

---

question_text:
A 2-year-old boy is brought to a GP in Warrnambool, Vic, at 9 pm with a barking cough and hoarse voice that started that evening, after two days of a runny nose. He has soft stridor only when he is upset. There is no stridor at rest, no chest wall recession, and he is alert and playing. SpO2 98%.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate management?
options: A single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg and discharge with safety-net advice
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. A single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg and discharge with safety-net advice

---

RCH guidance for mild croup (stridor only when upset) is a single dose of oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg, or prednisolone 1 mg/kg. Steroids reduce reattendance and shorten symptoms. A barking cough with no stridor at all does not need steroids. Nebulised adrenaline is for severe croup.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Croup with stridor: oral dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg. Nebulised adrenaline only for severe croup.

---

question_text:
A 20-month-old girl is brought to an emergency department in Gosford, NSW, after a 2-minute generalised tonic–clonic seizure at home during a fever. She had a runny nose for two days. She is now alert, interactive and back to normal. Temperature 39.0°C. There is no neck stiffness, rash or focal neurological signs, and she is fully immunised.

Which one of the following investigations is most appropriate?
options: Full blood count, electrolytes and blood culture
No routine investigations; look for the source of the fever clinically
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. No routine investigations; look for the source of the fever clinically

---

This is a simple febrile seizure. RCH guidelines state that investigations are low yield and not routinely needed. Assess for the focus of the fever clinically. Investigations are targeted only for atypical or complex seizures or a suspected serious infection.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Simple febrile seizure in a well child: no routine tests; find the fever source clinically.

---

question_text:
A 4-year-old boy in Hobart, Tas, has had puffy eyes for one week and now has swollen legs. BP is normal. Urinalysis shows 4+ protein with no blood. Serum albumin is 15 g/L, creatinine is normal and complement is normal. A diagnosis of likely steroid-sensitive nephrotic syndrome is made. He weighs 18 kg (body surface area 0.74 m²).

Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
options: Prednisolone 60 mg/m² daily for 4 weeks, then 40 mg/m² on alternate days for 4 weeks
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Prednisolone 60 mg/m² daily for 4 weeks, then 40 mg/m² on alternate days for 4 weeks

---

RCH guidelines for a first presentation recommend prednisolone 60 mg/m² (or 2 mg/kg, maximum 60 mg) daily for 4 weeks, then 40 mg/m² (or 1.5 mg/kg, maximum 40 mg) on alternate days for 4 weeks. A renal biopsy is not routinely needed in typical cases at this age.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
First-episode nephrotic syndrome: prednisolone 60 mg/m² daily for 4 weeks, then 40 mg/m² alternate days for 4 weeks.

---

question_text:
A 4-week-old breastfed boy is brought to a GP in Kalgoorlie, WA, because he is still jaundiced. He is feeding well and gaining weight. His mother thinks his stools have been pale for a week. His urine is dark yellow.

Investigations:
- Total bilirubin 160 µmol/L
- Conjugated bilirubin 70 µmol/L
- Liver ultrasound: normal liver; gallbladder seen

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next step?
options: Urgent same-day discussion and referral to paediatric gastroenterology
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Urgent same-day discussion and referral to paediatric gastroenterology

---

A conjugated bilirubin above 20 µmol/L (or more than 20% of the total) is abnormal, and with pale stools it suggests biliary atresia until proven otherwise. RCH guidelines state that a normal ultrasound does not exclude biliary atresia. Urgent referral matters because outcomes of Kasai surgery are better when it is done early.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Prolonged jaundice with conjugated bilirubin above 20 µmol/L or pale stools needs urgent gastroenterology referral. A normal US does not exclude biliary atresia.

---

question_text:
A 5-year-old girl is brought to an emergency department in Geraldton, WA, with one day of refusing to walk on her right leg. Temperature 38.9°C. She holds her hip flexed and externally rotated and resists all movement.

Investigations:
- WCC 17.8 × 10⁹/L
- CRP 96 mg/L
- ESR 55 mm/h
- Hip ultrasound: effusion

Which one of the following is the most appropriate interpretation and plan?
options: Likely septic arthritis; urgent orthopaedic review for joint aspiration and washout
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Likely septic arthritis; urgent orthopaedic review for joint aspiration and washout

---

RCH guidelines describe septic arthritis as an orthopaedic emergency. An effusion on ultrasound does not distinguish septic arthritis from transient synovitis, but fever, refusal to bear weight and raised WCC, CRP and ESR all point to infection. She needs urgent orthopaedic referral for aspiration and washout, with IV antibiotics given after cultures are taken.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
A febrile child who won't bear weight and has raised markers and an effusion has septic arthritis until proven otherwise; it is an orthopaedic emergency.

---

question_text:
A 9-year-old boy with asthma eats a muesli bar containing peanut at school camp near Kiama, NSW. Within 10 minutes he has hives, lip swelling, a hoarse voice, wheeze and difficulty breathing. A nurse is present with an adrenaline autoinjector, salbutamol and oral antihistamine.

Which one of the following should be given first?
options: Intramuscular adrenaline into the outer thigh
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Intramuscular adrenaline into the outer thigh

---

He has anaphylaxis with respiratory involvement. RCH guidelines say IM adrenaline must be given first, and in a child with asthma, adrenaline comes before any asthma medicine. Antihistamines and steroids should not be given as treatment of anaphylaxis. Adrenaline should not be given subcutaneously.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Anaphylaxis in a child with asthma: IM adrenaline first, before salbutamol.

---

question_text:
A 29-year-old man sees his GP in Perth, WA, after three emergency department visits in four months with sudden episodes of palpitations, chest tightness, tingling and fear of dying, each lasting about 15 minutes. ECG, troponin, TSH and full blood count were normal each time. He now avoids trains in case an attack happens. He drinks little alcohol and uses no drugs.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate first-line treatment?
options: Referral to cardiology for Holter monitoring
Cognitive behavioural therapy including interoceptive and in-vivo exposure
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

D. Cognitive behavioural therapy including interoceptive and in-vivo exposure

---

This is panic disorder with avoidance. CBT, including psychoeducation, interoceptive exposure and graded in-vivo exposure, is first-line. An SSRI is an alternative or can be added. Benzodiazepines are not recommended for ongoing treatment. A mental health treatment plan gives access to Medicare-subsidised psychology.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
First-line treatment for panic disorder is CBT with exposure, with an SSRI as an alternative or addition. Avoid benzodiazepines.

---

question_text:
A 26-year-old man with schizophrenia is reviewed by a community mental health team in Footscray, Vic. He still has persistent persecutory delusions and auditory hallucinations that impair his functioning. He has had an adequate trial of risperidone (6 weeks at 4 mg daily, confirmed adherent with a long-acting injection), followed by an adequate trial of olanzapine (8 weeks at 20 mg daily). He does not use substances.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate next treatment?
options: Clozapine with haematological and cardiac monitoring
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Clozapine with haematological and cardiac monitoring

---

He meets criteria for treatment-resistant schizophrenia (two adequate antipsychotic trials have failed). The RANZCP-endorsed INTEGRATE guidelines recommend starting clozapine promptly. Monitoring includes full blood count/neutrophils, troponin and CRP for myocarditis, and plasma levels with a target of 350–500 ng/mL. Metformin should be started alongside to limit weight gain.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
After two adequate antipsychotic trials fail, start clozapine promptly with monitoring.

question_text:
A 32-year-old woman presents to a hospital in Logan, Qld, with sudden weakness of her right leg that began after a stressful week at work. She can barely lift her right leg off the bed. When she is asked to flex her left hip against resistance, strong involuntary extension of the right hip is felt. Reflexes are symmetrical, plantar responses are flexor and sensation is normal. MRI of the brain and spine is normal.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate interpretation?
options: Positive Hoover sign consistent with functional neurological disorder
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Positive Hoover sign consistent with functional neurological disorder

---

A positive Hoover sign means hip extension is weak when tested directly but returns to normal during contralateral hip flexion. It is a positive clinical sign of functional weakness. FND is diagnosed on positive features, not by exclusion alone. It is not feigning. Treatment involves explaining the diagnosis clearly, then physiotherapy and psychological therapy.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Hoover sign is a positive sign of functional weakness. FND is diagnosed on positive features, and it is not feigning.

question_text:
A 20-year-old university student in Newcastle, NSW, tells her GP she binge-eats several times a week and then makes herself vomit. Her BMI is 22 kg/m². She has bilateral parotid swelling and calluses on the backs of her fingers. She feels lightheaded at times.

Which one of the following investigations is most important at this visit?
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Serum electrolytes including potassium

---

Self-induced vomiting causes hypokalaemic, hypochloraemic metabolic alkalosis, which can lead to arrhythmias. Electrolytes, including potassium, should be checked, and an ECG done if potassium is low. Treatment is eating-disorder-focused CBT (CBT-E), and a Medicare eating disorder plan is available.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
In bulimia with purging, check potassium (hypokalaemic alkalosis can cause arrhythmia).

---

question_text:
An 84-year-old woman with Alzheimer disease in a residential aged care facility in Launceston, Tas, has become agitated in the late afternoons over two weeks, calling out and pacing. Physical examination, urinalysis and a review of her medicines show no delirium, pain or constipation. Staff ask for 'something to settle her'.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate initial management?
options: Person-centred non-pharmacological strategies such as an individualised routine, activity and environmental changes
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

C. Person-centred non-pharmacological strategies such as an individualised routine, activity and environmental changes

The NSW Health BPSD guidance advises non-pharmacological management first, after excluding physical causes. Medication (risperidone is the antipsychotic most often used, and only for a time-limited period) is considered only when the behaviour is severe and other measures have not been enough.

In BPSD, manage non-pharmacologically first, after excluding physical causes.

question_text:
A 58-year-old man in Toowoomba, Qld, has taken oxazepam 30 mg three times daily for six years. It was first prescribed after a bereavement. He would now like to stop. He has no history of seizures and does not drink alcohol.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate plan?
options: Switch to an equivalent dose of diazepam and reduce gradually over weeks to months
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. Switch to an equivalent dose of diazepam and reduce gradually over weeks to months

---

Stopping benzodiazepines abruptly after long-term use risks withdrawal seizures. Australian Prescriber advises a gradual dose reduction over weeks to months, often after switching to diazepam because its long half-life gives a smoother taper.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Stop long-term benzodiazepines with a slow taper, often after switching to diazepam.

---

question_text:
A new point-of-care test for deep vein thrombosis has a sensitivity of 90% and a specificity of 70% compared with compression ultrasound.

Which one of the following is the positive likelihood ratio of this test?
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. 3.0

---

LR+ = sensitivity ÷ (1 − specificity) = 0.90 ÷ 0.30 = 3.0. A positive result triples the pre-test odds.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
LR+ = sensitivity ÷ (1 − specificity).

---

REFERENCES

question_text:
A case–control study in Victoria compares mothers of infants born with a congenital heart defect with mothers of healthy infants. All are asked months after the birth about over-the-counter medicines they took in early pregnancy. Case mothers report more medicine use.

Which one of the following biases is most likely to explain part of this association?
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. Recall bias

---

Mothers of affected infants are more likely to search their memories and report exposures. This differential misclassification of exposure is recall bias, and it is typical of case–control studies that rely on self-report.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
Self-reported past exposures in case–control studies are prone to recall bias.

---

question_text:
In a cohort of 2,000 Queensland farm workers followed for 5 years, 1,000 worked regularly with livestock and 1,000 did not. Leptospirosis was diagnosed in 20 livestock workers and 5 non-livestock workers.

Which one of the following is the relative risk of leptospirosis for livestock work?
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

E. 4.0

---

RR = (20/1000) ÷ (5/1000) = 0.02 ÷ 0.005 = 4.0.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
RR = risk in the exposed ÷ risk in the unexposed.

question_text:
A 45-year-old woman who is a Jehovah's Witness is admitted to a Melbourne hospital with heavy menstrual bleeding. Her haemoglobin is 62 g/L. She has full decision-making capacity. After a clear discussion of the risks, including death, she refuses any transfusion of blood products. She carries a signed advance care directive refusing blood.

Which one of the following is the most appropriate course of action?
options: Respect her refusal and use blood-sparing alternatives such as IV iron and treatment of the bleeding
Discharge her because she is refusing treatment
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

B. Respect her refusal and use blood-sparing alternatives such as IV iron and treatment of the bleeding

---

A competent adult may refuse any treatment, including treatment that would save her life, and a valid advance directive must be respected. Use alternatives such as IV iron, tranexamic acid, hormonal or surgical control of the bleeding, and cell salvage if she accepts it. Document the discussion carefully.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
A competent adult's refusal of blood, including in a valid advance directive, must be respected. Use blood-sparing alternatives.

---

A 46-year-old woman sees her GP in Darwin, NT, with a new 2 cm firm lump in her left breast that she noticed three weeks ago. She asks whether she should book a free BreastScreen mammogram.

Book BreastScreen because she is over 40

A 23-year-old woman starting work at an abattoir in Wagga Wagga, NSW, attends for Q fever vaccination. Pre-vaccination testing shows a negative Q fever antibody serology, and the skin test, read 7 days later, is positive (induration 6 mm).

Which one of the following is the most appropriate interpretation and action?
options: She is sensitised and should not be vaccinated
Repeat the skin test in 1 week
explanation:
CORRECT ANSWER

A. She is sensitised and should not be vaccinated

---

The Australian Immunisation Handbook states that a positive result on either serology or skin test means the person is sensitised and must not be vaccinated, because of the risk of severe local reactions. Vaccination goes ahead only if both tests are negative.

---

KEY LEARNING POINT
